title: Ancient enemies
hookLine: 'that's just how i am': Shantideva agrees the enemies are old, and still says they can be driven out
tomorrow: so how does a warrior actually stand against a craving?

cards: That's just how I am. People say it about running late, about a short fuse, about biting their nails since second grade. Sometimes it's honest.

Sometimes it's a door being quietly locked from the inside. If a habit has lived in you for years, it can feel like furniture, part of the house. Shantideva has an answer, and it isn't the comforting one you might expect.
First he agrees: yes, these enemies are very old. Then he says something that sounds impossible.

teach.h: NO BEGINNING, NO END IN SIGHT.
teach.b: Here's his first move. Ordinary enemies don't last long, he says. These have no beginning and no end in sight.
And worse: serve an ordinary enemy and they may turn friendly; serve these, and they only hurt you more. So two views open up, and Buddhists hold both.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: TAKE THE AGE SERIOUSLY.
teach.b: View one: take the age seriously. Afflictions run deep. Craving has been at work through countless lives, tradition teaches, and anyone who promises it'll vanish by Friday is selling something.
Patience with the long road is part of the path. View two: old isn't the same as you. In the Pali suttas, the Buddha calls the mind luminous, stained by defilements that arrive as visitors.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: A STAIN ISN'T THE WINDOW.
teach.b: A stain on a window isn't the window. The best case for each? The first keeps you humble and steady when the habit comes back.
The second keeps you hopeful when it seems permanent. Shantideva stands in both. Ancient, yes.
But he still says one can drive them out, because what's built of causes can come apart when the causes change.

how: Buddhists speak of afflictions both as deep habits carried over many lives, to be worked with patiently, and as passing stains on a mind that is clear by nature; teachers often hold the two together.

o: afflictions so old they feel permanent, yet removable
rival families who have feuded for generations
the first sins described at the start of the world

games.q: two views, one verse — tap the pairs.
p: don't last long; can turn friendly
no beginning, no end in sight

s: if a habit is very old, Buddhism says it's part of who you are
Shantideva calls them ancient and still says they can be driven out.
in the Pali suttas the Buddha calls the mind luminous, stained by visiting defilements
the stains arrive; they aren't the mind itself.

games.q: your friend has snapped at people when stressed for as long as anyone remembers. she says 'that's just me, i'll never change.' which reply holds both views?
o: it's deep and old, so be patient with yourself, and it can still loosen.
you're right, a temper that old is just part of who you are.
if you really wanted to, you'd stop snapping by this weekend.
games.why: Shantideva holds both: the enemies are ancient, and they can go. old means patient work, not a life sentence.

practice: Choose one old habit you'd like to loosen. Name what you wish for instead, then the moment it usually wins, like the second you sit on the couch.
Then make a plan in one sentence: when that moment comes, I'll do this one small thing. Hold the plan in mind for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Ancient enemies: the afflictions, old beyond counting, Shantideva says. Old enough to respect, and still not part of the furniture.

orig.note: Sanskrit: beginningless, without a first point; used of the afflictions and of the round of rebirth.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: they can go, even the ones that feel like they've always been there. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 4.33-4.35 (these enemies are long-lasting, without beginning or end; served, other enemies become friendly, these only harm more) and 4.44-4.46 (they can be driven out)
Anguttara Nikaya 1.49-1.52 (the mind is luminous, defiled by incoming defilements)
